I don't fit in and everyone will notice

I'm fundamentally different in a bad way
coherence_explanation: The thought-emotion chain is highly coherent. conversation: Therapist: How are you?
Patient: Hey! I'm doing okay, I guess. Just been a bit in my head lately if I'm being honest. Work's been fine, but there's this thing that's been kind of bugging me.

Therapist: Thank you for sharing that. I appreciate your openness. It sounds like something's been on your mind—that "thing" that's bugging you. I'd like to understand what's going on for you better. Could you tell me a bit more about what's been bothering you? What specifically has been occupying your thoughts?

Patient: Yeah, so... you know how my coworker invited me to their birthday party? It's this weekend. And I just... I haven't even responded yet. It's been like a week since they asked.

I know I should just say yes or no, but honestly I'm kinda dreading it. Like, I keep thinking about going and I just get this knot in my stomach, you know? I've been looking at the invite over and over, checking who all is gonna be there, and just... I don't know. My brain keeps running through all these scenarios of how awkward it's gonna be.

Therapist: I hear you—there's a real physical response happening when you think about this party, that knot in your stomach. That tells me something deeper is going on beneath the surface. 

I want to explore this with you a bit. When you say you're running through scenarios of how awkward it'll be, what specifically are you imagining happening? Like, when you picture yourself at this party, what's the worst-case scenario playing out in your mind?

Patient: Ugh, okay so like... I picture myself just standing there, and everyone's already talking and laughing, and I just... I don't know what to say, you know? Like I'll open my mouth and nothing will come out, or I'll say something stupid and everyone will just look at me weird.

And then I'm thinking like, people are probably already judging me for not responding for a week. They're probably like "why is this person so awkward?" Like they'll see through me or something and just think I'm... I don't know, weird? Out of place?

The worst part is I keep imagining myself just standing in the corner trying to look busy, or making up an excuse to leave early. Like, I know everyone else will just be fine, having a good time, and I'll be the one person who doesn't fit in. Everyone will notice.

That's why I've been avoiding actually hitting reply. Because once I say yes, it becomes real, you know?

Therapist: Thank you for being so specific with me—that really helps me understand what's happening. So I'm hearing a few interconnected thoughts here: that you'll say something "stupid" and be judged, that people are already judging you for not responding, and underneath all of that is this belief that you don't fit in and that everyone will *notice*. 

I want to gently point something out: you're predicting pretty confidently what other people are thinking and feeling—that they're judging you, that they'll see through you. But here's my question: **How do you actually know that's true?** What evidence do you have that people are already thinking negatively about you, versus that being something your anxiety is telling you? 

And I'm also curious—when you say "everyone else will just be fine"—do you think those people at the party have ever felt awkward or out of place? Or is it possible they experience some of what you're experiencing but you just don't see it?

Patient: Hmm, okay that's... yeah, that's a good point actually.

I mean, when I really think about it, I don't *know* they're judging me. Like, my coworker invited me, right? So they obviously want me there. And now that you mention it... I guess people probably do feel awkward sometimes. Like, I remember my friend Sarah saying she hated parties because she never knew what to talk about either.

It's just... when I'm in my head about this, it *feels* like everyone's watching and judging. It feels so real. Like my brain is just convinced that I'm the weird one, that I don't belong there.

But like... logically I know that might not be totally true. I just can't shake the feeling, you know? Even knowing that, I'm still like dreading it and avoiding the invite.

And honestly, I haven't even given myself a chance to actually go and see what happens. I'm just assuming the worst based on... what? My anxiety? Like why am I so sure I'll embarrass myself when I haven't even tried?

Therapist: This is a really important realization you're having right now. You're noticing the gap between what your anxiety is telling you and what you actually know to be true—and that's powerful. You're right that you're assuming the worst without any real evidence, and you haven't given yourself a chance to actually experience the party.

Here's what I want to highlight: your anxiety feels *certain*, but certainty isn't the same as truth. Your brain is protecting you from perceived threat by catastrophizing—but the cost is avoidance, which actually keeps the anxiety alive.

So let me ask you this: **What if you went to this party and—even if you felt awkward for part of it—you didn't embarrass yourself?** What if you just... showed up and let yourself be human? Not perfect, not the life of the party, just present?

And here's the harder question: **What would happen if you did say something awkward? What's actually the worst outcome?** We need to look at that fear directly, because right now you're avoiding based on a feeling, not based on reality.

Patient: Wow, okay... I'm like sitting with that for a second.

If I actually went and didn't embarrass myself? I guess... I'd feel relieved? Maybe even proud of myself for actually showing up instead of making an excuse. And like, maybe I'd realize it wasn't as bad as my brain made it out to be.

But the thing is... even if I *did* say something awkward, like genuinely awkward... what's the actual worst that happens? People would maybe laugh awkwardly for a second and then move on? Or they'd think "oh that was kinda weird" and then just... keep talking about something else?

It's not like anyone's gonna like, hate me forever or kick me out or something. I guess when I say it out loud it sounds kind of silly, but my brain is still like "but what if though?"

I think the real thing I'm scared of is like... proving to myself that I don't belong? Or like, that people can see that I'm not as... together as everyone else. That I'm just fundamentally different in a bad way.

But you're right—I've been avoiding this for a week based on feelings, not facts. And the avoidance is actually making the anxiety worse because now I'm like stressed about *not* responding too.

What do you think I should do?

Therapist: I'm really glad you're seeing this clearly now. But here's the thing—I can't tell you what to do, because the real work happens when *you* decide. What I can tell you is this: you've just done something crucial. You've identified the core fear underneath all of this: that you're fundamentally different in a bad way, that you don't belong. That's the real anxiety driving the avoidance.

The question isn't whether you "should" go to the party. The question is: **Are you willing to test out what you're believing?** Are you willing to gather real evidence instead of trusting the predictions your anxiety is making?

Here's what I'd suggest: Instead of trying to be perfect or prove you belong, what if you went with the simple goal of staying for 30 minutes and just observing? Notice who talks to you. Notice if anyone actually judges you. Notice if the worst actually happens. Give yourself permission to feel awkward *and* still be there.

The avoidance keeps the fear alive. But showing up—even imperfectly—that's how you actually challenge this belief that you don't belong.

So what feels true for you right now? Do you want to test this out, or is the anxiety still winning?

Patient: You know what... yeah. I think I need to actually do this.

Like, I've been letting my brain run the show for a week and it's not helping anything. I'm still anxious, I haven't responded, and now I'm stressed about that too. So like... what's the point of avoiding if it's not even making me feel better?

I think I'm gonna respond to the invite. Say yes. And I'll go with that plan—just 30 minutes, see what actually happens instead of what my brain thinks will happen.

It's still scary to say that out loud, but I think you're right. The only way I'm gonna know if I actually belong or if I'm as awkward as I think is to actually... go and find out. And like, worst case scenario I stay 30 minutes, realize it's not terrible, and I can stay longer or leave. Either way I showed up.

I'm gonna do it before I chicken out though. Like, right now. I'm gonna text back and say I'm coming.

That's the move, right?

Therapist: That's exactly the move. Right now, before the anxiety can talk you out of it. Send that text. And when you do, notice how you feel—there might be some relief mixed in with the nervousness, and that's important. You're taking your power back from anxiety.

One thing to remember as the weekend approaches: you might still feel anxious *before* the party, and that's okay. Anxiety doesn't mean you're making the wrong choice. It just means you're doing something brave. The goal isn't to feel calm—it's to go anyway and gather real evidence.

I'm really proud of you for deciding to test this out. This is how change actually happens. Let's check in after the party and see what you actually discover about yourself and whether people are really judging you the way your brain predicted.

Patient: Okay, I'm gonna do it right now. Like literally about to send the text.

And yeah, I get it—the anxiety might still be there, but I'm going anyway. That's the whole point, right? I'm not waiting to feel calm. I'm just... going.

Thanks for like, actually breaking this down with me instead of just telling me I'm being silly or whatever. It helps to actually *see* where my brain's been messing with me, you know?

I'll definitely let you know how it goes. Honestly I'm nervous but also like... a little bit hopeful? Which is different from this week where I've just been dreading it.

Okay, sending the text now. Wish me luck lol.

Therapist: That's it—send it! You've got this. And I love that you're feeling hopeful instead of just dread. That shift matters. You're not waiting for courage to come to you; you're being courageous right now by facing this head-on. That's the real work.

Go text your coworker. And when you're at that party, remember: you belong there because you chose to show up. Everything else is just your brain learning that the world doesn't end when things feel awkward. You're gonna gather some real evidence this weekend.

Can't wait to hear how it goes. You've already won by deciding to try.

Patient: Thanks, really. I needed that push honestly. Okay, doing it now—no more overthinking.

I'll hit you up after the weekend and let you know what actually happened versus what my anxiety was screaming at me about. Hopefully I'll have some good news lol, or at least proof that I survived and the world didn't end.

Talk soon. And thanks again for not letting me just spiral—that actually helped.

Therapist: You're welcome—and I'm genuinely proud of you for taking action. You've done the hardest part already: recognizing the pattern and choosing to face it anyway. That takes real courage. Go send that text, and remember—you don't need to be perfect at that party, just present. I'm looking forward to hearing what you discover about yourself this weekend. You've got this. Talk soon!

Patient: Alright, I'm doing it. Text sent. 

Honestly feels kinda surreal that I just committed to going, but also like... relief? Mixed with nervous energy, but you were right—that's okay.

I'm gonna go before my brain tries to convince me to unsend it lol. Thanks for real though. I'll text you after the party with the update.

See you soon! 👍

Therapist: That's amazing—text sent! That relief you're feeling? That's you taking your power back. Now go before the anxiety tries to convince you otherwise. Enjoy the rest of your day knowing you've already done the brave thing. Can't wait to hear how the party goes. You've got this. 👍

Patient: Perfect. I'm out—gonna distract myself with something else so I don't spiral before the weekend lol.

Thanks again. Seriously. I'll be back after to tell you how it went.

Talk soon! ✌️
Therapist: You've got this! Go live your weekend and come back with the real story instead of the anxiety story. See you after! ✌️
Patient: Will do. Thanks for keeping me real. Catch you after the party! 👋

Therapist: Great work taking action today. Enjoy your weekend, and I'll be here when you're ready to debrief. You've already proven to yourself that you can face the anxiety—now go experience what actually happens. See you after the party! 👋

If I'm not perfect, then I'm a fraud who doesn't belong here

coherence_explanation: The thought-to-emotion chain is coherent and well-established. The patient's automatic thoughts ("I'm going to get fired," "Everyone thinks I'm incompetent," "This proves I'm not good enough for this job," "If I'm not perfect, then I'm a fraud") logically lead to the emotions of anxiety, panic, dread, shame, and inadequacy. The therapist correctly identified that catastrophic thoughts about job security and competence would naturally produce fear and shame responses. However, there's a minor gap: the patient also mentions "terror" and "worthless" feelings that could have been explored more explicitly as distinct from just "anxiety" and "inadequacy."

conversation: Therapist: How are you?
Patient: Hey, I'm doing okay... well, trying to be anyway. Just been a bit in my head lately. Had this thing happen at work yesterday that I can't really shake, you know?

Therapist: I hear you—it sounds like something from work is weighing on you. I'd like to understand what happened. Can you tell me more about what occurred yesterday that you're having trouble letting go of?

Patient: Yeah, so I was giving a presentation to the team and I made this small mistake—like, nothing huge in the grand scheme of things. But my manager just said "we can discuss this later" and... I don't know, man. That one comment has just been eating at me ever since.

I keep replaying the whole thing in my head, going over what I said, what I could've done differently. And now I'm like... what if they're all thinking I'm totally incompetent? Like, does this one slip-up mean I'm not actually cut out for this job?

I've been staying late trying to make up for it somehow, and honestly I've been avoiding going into my manager's office. Which is weird because normally that's not a big deal. I don't know, it just feels like this could be a bigger thing than it probably is.

Therapist: I can really hear how much this is affecting you, and I appreciate you sharing that. What strikes me is there's a big gap between what actually happened—a small mistake—and how much mental energy you're spending on it. That tells me something deeper might be going on here.

Let me ask you this: when your manager said "we can discuss this later," what was the very first thought that went through your mind? Not the spiraling thoughts that came after, but that immediate gut reaction—what did you tell yourself that meant?

Patient: Oh man, okay so... my immediate thought was literally "I'm going to get fired." Like that was instant, right? 

And then it snowballed from there into "everyone thinks I'm incompetent" and "this proves I'm not good enough for this job." It's wild because I *know* logically that one small mistake doesn't get you fired, but in that moment it felt so real, you know?

I guess underneath all that, there's this voice saying like... if I'm not perfect, then what? Like, any mistake means I messed up. And if I can't be perfect at my job, then maybe I really am just a fraud and don't belong here.

It's exhausting honestly. Because even when things go well, I'm always worried the next thing is gonna expose me or prove that I'm actually not as capable as people think. One slip and suddenly it feels like everything is on the line.

Therapist: Thank you for being so honest about that—that's really valuable. So what I'm hearing is a pretty rigid rule you're operating under: "If I'm not perfect, then I'm a fraud who doesn't belong here." And when you made that small mistake, it felt like proof of that belief rather than just... a normal human mistake.

Here's what I want to explore with you: Where do you think that voice—the one saying you need to be perfect to have worth—where does that come from? Can you think back to earlier in your life, maybe growing up, where you learned that mistakes meant you weren't good enough?

And second, I'm curious: have there been times in your job where you *weren't* perfect, but nothing catastrophic happened? Times that contradict this fear?

Patient: Hmm, yeah that's hitting something for me. Growing up, my parents were always pretty critical. Like, good grades weren't celebrated—they were expected. If I got a B, it was "why not an A?" That kind of thing. I think I internalized pretty early that my value was tied to performing flawlessly, you know? Mess up and you're not trying hard enough.

As for the job thing... honestly, yeah. I've made mistakes before and nothing terrible happened. Like last quarter I miscalculated some numbers in a report and we caught it, fixed it, moved on. My manager didn't even mention it again. And I've heard colleagues make mistakes all the time and everyone just... helps them fix it or laughs it off.

But here's the weird part—when I remember that stuff, it doesn't actually comfort me? Like I *know* intellectually that mistakes happen, but when I'm in the moment like I was yesterday, that knowledge just disappears. It's like my brain goes straight to catastrophe mode instead of "okay, this is fixable."

And I've been checking job postings too, which is so dumb because I don't even want to leave. I think part of me is like... if I jump ship first, at least I'm not getting fired, you know?

Therapist: You've just identified something really important—there's a split happening in you between what you *know* logically and what you *feel* emotionally. That checking job postings thing? That's not dumb at all. That's your anxiety trying to take control by getting ahead of the perceived threat. It's like saying "I'll leave before they can fire me," which gives a false sense of safety, but it keeps the cycle going.

Here's what I want to point out: You have evidence that contradicts this catastrophe narrative—the report error, colleagues making mistakes—but anxiety doesn't care about evidence in the moment. It cares about protection. So the real work here is understanding *why* your brain defaults to catastrophe mode when you're triggered, even when you have proof it's not accurate.

Let me ask you something: When you're in that catastrophe spiral, it feels *certain*, right? Like it's not a thought—it feels like a fact. Does it feel that way?

Patient: Yeah, exactly. It feels like absolute fact in the moment. Like I'm not *thinking* "maybe they'll fire me"—it feels like I'm stating something that's obviously true, you know? It's not a question mark, it's like my brain has already decided what's happening.

And that's what makes it so hard to shake. Even when I logically know better, the feeling is so strong and so immediate that it overrides everything else. It's like my body is in full panic mode before my brain can even catch up and be like "wait, hold on."

That's probably why I can't stop replaying the presentation either. I think part of me is searching for... I don't know, proof that it wasn't that bad? Or proof that I *am* actually competent? But it just keeps feeding the spiral instead.

It's frustrating because I *want* to just move on and be chill about it like a normal person, but I can't seem to turn it off. And the more I try not to think about it, the more I think about it.

Last night I almost texted my manager just to preemptively explain myself, which would've been such a bad move. I stopped myself but like... that shows you where my head's at, right?

Therapist: You've really mapped this out clearly, and I want to validate something: what you're describing—that feeling of certainty, the panic before logic catches up, the compulsive replaying and urge to text your manager—that's all your nervous system in threat mode. And the behaviors you're doing (ruminating, checking job postings, staying late, avoiding your manager) *temporarily* feel like they're helping, but they're actually teaching your brain that the threat is real. Each time you avoid or reassure-seek, anxiety goes "see? I was right to be worried."

Here's what we're going to work on: We can't make the anxious thought disappear through willpower or logic alone—that's been clear to you. But we *can* change your relationship to it. Instead of fighting the thought or trying to prove it wrong, we learn to notice it, acknowledge it as a thought your anxiety is producing (not a fact), and act according to what actually matters to you—not what fear is telling you.

Before we go deeper into techniques, I want to ask: What would you be doing differently right now if that presentation mistake hadn't happened? What's the version of yourself you actually want to be at work?

Patient: Oh man, that's a good question. I think... I'd just be normal, you know? Like I'd probably have mentioned it to my manager casually at some point—just owned it, fixed it, moved on. I wouldn't be dreading the conversation.

The version of me I actually want to be is someone who can mess up, learn from it, and not spiral into thinking it means everything is falling apart. Someone who can walk into my manager's office without my chest tightening. Someone who trusts that one mistake doesn't define me or my entire career.

Honestly, I think I'd be focusing on actual work instead of obsessing over this. I wouldn't be staying late out of panic—I'd just do my job and then actually enjoy my evening, you know? Maybe hang out with friends without my brain being stuck on replay mode.

And I definitely wouldn't be doom-scrolling through job postings at 11 PM pretending I'm casually looking when really I'm just scared.

I guess the real thing is... I want to feel secure enough in myself that one mistake feels manageable instead of like proof that I don't belong. That's the big one.

Therapist: That clarity you just expressed—that's exactly what we're working toward. You want to be someone who can handle mistakes without it threatening your sense of belonging. That's a realistic, achievable goal, and honestly, you're already showing self-awareness that most people take years to develop.

Here's what I want you to sit with: The work isn't about forcing yourself to "be chill" or thinking positive. It's about building tolerance for the discomfort of uncertainty. Right now, when anxiety says "you might get fired," you treat it like an emergency that needs solving immediately. Instead, we're going to practice letting that thought exist without acting on it.

Before our next session, I'd like you to do something: This week, notice when you get the urge to avoid your manager or check those job postings or replay the presentation. Don't judge yourself—just observe it. Ask yourself: "What am I trying to protect myself from right now?" Write down what comes up. We'll use that to understand the pattern better.

Also—and this is important—I want you to schedule that conversation with your manager. Not because you need to prove anything, but because avoidance is what keeps anxiety alive. You've survived difficult conversations before. This one won't be different.

How does that feel?

Patient: Honestly? It feels both doable and terrifying at the same time, which I guess means it's the right thing to do, huh?

The observation thing—yeah, I can do that. It'll probably be eye-opening to see how many times a day I'm actually doing this stuff without even realizing it. And writing it down might help me see the pattern more clearly instead of just being stuck in my head.

But scheduling the conversation... *exhales* okay, that's the one that's hitting different. Like, logically I know it needs to happen and it'll probably be fine, but my gut is still like "nope, don't do it." That's the avoidance thing you're talking about, right? That feeling of dread is telling me to put it off, which then makes it worse.

I think I'm gonna do it though. Like, not today because I'll psych myself out, but maybe tomorrow morning before I overthink it? Just send a quick message asking when they have time to chat. Short and simple.

And then I'll probably be anxious about it until it happens, which sucks, but I get that that's kind of the point—learning that I can feel scared and do it anyway.

Thanks for helping me see this stuff more clearly. It's weirdly comforting knowing this is actually a recognizable pattern instead of just me being broken.

Therapist: You're not broken—you're having a very human response to perfectionism and threat. What you just said—"I can feel scared and do it anyway"—that's actually the core of what we're building. Tomorrow morning is perfect. Keep it simple: "Hey, when would be a good time to talk about the presentation?" That's it. Your job isn't to be calm; it's just to do it while feeling the fear. And then we'll debrief on what happened. You've got this.

Patient: Yeah, okay. I'm gonna do it tomorrow morning. I'll just send the message and sit with the uncomfortable feeling instead of trying to make it go away. That actually feels less exhausting than what I've been doing—all the avoidance and obsessing is way more draining anyway.

I really appreciate this, honestly. Just talking through it and seeing it mapped out helps. Like, I can see the cycle now instead of just being trapped in it. And knowing that this is something I can actually work on—that there are actual steps to take—that's huge for me.

I'll keep that journal thing going too. Notice the patterns, write them down, see what I'm protecting myself from. I'm curious what'll come up when I actually pay attention to it instead of just running on autopilot.

Talk soon?

Therapist: Absolutely, I'm really glad you're feeling more clarity. You've done great work here today—recognizing the pattern, understanding where it comes from, and most importantly, committing to moving toward what you actually want instead of running from fear. That takes real courage.

So here's what you've got: Send that message tomorrow morning, sit with the discomfort, and keep that journal of when you notice the urge to avoid or reassure-seek. Write down what you're protecting yourself from each time. When we talk next, we'll look at those patterns together and start building some concrete tools to interrupt the cycle.

Remember—anxiety will tell you a lot of scary stories. Your job isn't to believe them or disprove them. It's just to notice them and keep moving forward anyway. You've already proven you can do hard things.

Let's check in after that conversation happens. You've got this.

Patient: Thanks, really. I actually feel a bit lighter just from this conversation. Like there's a plan now instead of me just spinning in circles.

I'll text my manager tomorrow morning—no overthinking it. And I'll keep that journal going. I know anxiety's gonna try to convince me it's a bad idea right up until I hit send, but I get it now. That's just the pattern doing its thing.

I'm gonna try to be a bit gentler with myself this week too. Not beat myself up for the spiraling when it happens, just notice it and be like "oh, there's that again." 

Really looking forward to our next check-in. I'll let you know how the conversation goes. Thanks for making this make sense. Catch you soon.

Therapist: You're so welcome. You've really done the hard work here today, and I can hear the shift in how you're thinking about this. That lightness you're feeling? That's what happens when you move from being stuck *in* the anxiety to observing it. Keep that momentum.

Text your manager tomorrow morning, journal the urges, and be gentle with yourself when the spiraling happens—that self-compassion is crucial. You're building a new relationship with discomfort, and that takes practice.

I'm looking forward to hearing how the conversation goes. You know where to reach me. Take care of yourself this week.

Patient: Will do. Thanks again—seriously. I feel way more hopeful about this than I did when we started talking. 

I'll check in after I talk to my manager. Appreciate you, man. Talk soon.

Therapist: You're very welcome. I'm really glad you're feeling more hopeful—that's exactly where we want to be. You've got a solid plan, you understand the pattern, and most importantly, you're ready to act despite the anxiety. That's what matters. Go take care of yourself, send that message tomorrow, and I'll be here when you're ready to debrief. You've got this.
Patient: Yeah, I got it. Thanks for real. Gonna head out now and try to get a decent night's sleep for once. Catch you soon.

Therapist: Take care of yourself tonight. You've done great work here, and you're more prepared than you think. Get that rest, send that message tomorrow morning, and I'll be here for our next session. You've got this.
